newsitem.title: USA: Plane parts recovered from Colorado mountainside.
newsitem.headline: Plane parts recovered from Colorado mountainside.

text.p: An Air Force helicopter crewman recovered two small pieces of metal Wednesday from a snowy peak in the Rocky Mountains where wreckage of a warplane that disappeared three weeks ago is believed buried.
The parts -- a harness cable assembly and a piece believed to be from a military-type plane engine -- are being examined to determine if they came from the missing A-10 Thunderbolt.
"We are attempting to identify the parts to see if they are pieces of the A-10," Air Force Maj.-Gen. Nels Running told reporters.
"There is no clear label to say this came from an A-10, but our suspicions are getting closer and we hope in the near-term to tell you we have our A-10," he said.
Two A-10 pilots were at the rescue headquarters in Eagle, Colorado, to examine the pieces of wreckage.

Running said the crewman from an MH-53 heavy lift helicopter was lowered to the side of the mountain where wreckage was spotted. However, the largest piece of wreckage visible above through snow was too big to lift, he said.
The crewman found the two small pieces nearby and retrieved them for inspection. Both pieces bore "manufacturer's nomenclature" and other markings that could determine what plane they came from.
Running said clearing skies would allow the helicopter into the air again later in an effort to land more men at the crash site.
The A-10 Thunderbolt attack bomber is thought to have slammed into the side of the 12,500-foot (3,800-metre) -high New York Mountain in the remote Sawatch range southeast of the Vail ski resort.
The wreckage was spotted on Sunday by an Army National Guard helicopter crew near a steep cliff on New York Mountain.
The A-10 Thunderbolt disappeared during a routine training mission April 2.

Air Force officials have been at a loss to explain why the pilot, Capt. Craig Button, 32, left the three-plane delta formation in which he was flying and apparently veered northeast into Colorado, some 850 miles (1,350 km) away from a training exercise.

Button, whose plane was carrying four 500-pound (225-kg) Mark 82 conventional bombs, broke formation after leaving the Davis-Monthan Air Force Base near Tucson, Arizona, en route for the Barry M. Goldwater Bombing Range in Arizona.
